description: We are an ambitious team of four engineering students from Mansoura University, passionate about space exploration, data analysis, and innovative software solutions. We are ready to tackle the challenge and build something impactful!
summary:
SPACE EXPLORER — Outpost Survival is a browser-based educational game where players run a research outpost on the Moon or Mars. Players explore a map, build sites like solar arrays and greenhouses, manage limited resources each "sol," and face decision events with three graded options — where quick fixes trigger delayed penalties later. The game runs in two modes: Random Mode with unpredictable environmental events, and Historical Mode with 18 real NASA-documented scenarios such as the 1972 solar storm and the 2018 Mars dust storm.

It addresses the challenge by turning abstract resource management into a playable experience grounded in real science. Live NASA data (solar particle events, solar irradiance, radiation dose rates) drives gameplay, with archived fallbacks so the game never breaks. Two difficulty modes serve ages 7–12, and every screen clearly labels content as real data, scientific model, or game simulation.

It matters because it teaches children that every decision has a price, that science is about balancing trade-offs, and that space exploration is genuinely hard. Simple to play, honest about its science, and built to never break.
details: 1. What does it do, and how does it work?SPACE EXPLORER is a browser-based survival and decision-making game where players run a research outpost on the Moon or Mars. The player explores a 2D map, discovers sites (habitat, solar array, ice deposit, greenhouse, research lab, rover), builds them using limited resources, and then faces a stream of mission decisions — each with three graded options and real consequences.The core loop works like this:Explore the map to discover sites, then build them to generate resources each "sol" (one game day = one turn).Each sol, resources drain. The player picks a power plan (Crew Care, Shield Up, or Science) that trades one resource for another.Every two sols, a decision event appears. Options range from a cautious fix (costly now, safe later) to a quick patch (cheap now, delayed penalty a few turns later).The player wins by completing all missions and surviving a minimum number of sols; they lose if any critical resource hits zero.Two modes: Random Mode (unpredictable environmental events) and Historical Mode (18 real NASA-documented scenarios, such as the 1972 solar storm, the 2018 Mars dust storm, and the 2022 Marsquake).2. What benefits does it have?Teaches trade-off thinking. There is no perfect option — every choice has a cost. This mirrors real engineering decision-making.Connects play to real science. Game events are driven by live NASA data (solar particle events, solar irradiance, radiation dose rates) with documented archived fallbacks, so the game never breaks even offline.Accessible to a wide age range. Cadet mode uses only 3 core resources with bigger text and no jargon; Commander mode adds full science notes and tighter budgets.Supports struggling readers with a read-aloud feature.Teaches from failure. Every loss is linked to a specific science lesson the player can apply next time.Zero cost to run. All data sources are free and require no API keys, so it deploys instantly.Transparent about its science. Every screen labels content as NASA Recorded Data, Scientific Model, or Game Simulation — building trust rather than pretending.3. What is the intended impact?The goal is for a child to finish the game understanding three things:Every decision has a price — and short-term fixes often create long-term problems.Science is about balancing trade-offs, not memorizing answers.Space exploration is genuinely hard — and the difficulty comes from limited resources, radiation, dust, and communication delays, not from fantasy.On a broader level, the project aims to make real NASA data approachable and fun for young learners, and to show that educational games can be honest about what is real and what is simplified.4. What tools, languages, and software were used?HTML5 for structure and screensCSS3 for the visual theme, animations, responsive layout, and accessibility (large text, focus outlines, difficulty-based styling)Vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks) for all game logic — resource management, events, mission progression, save/loadBrowser localStorage for automatic save and resumeWeb Speech API for the read-aloud featureNASA public APIs (DONKI for solar particle events, POWER for solar irradiance, OSDR RadLab for radiation dose) — all free, no keys requiredArchived NASA data as a built-in fallback layerNo external libraries or paid services were needed, which keeps the project lightweight and deployable anywhere.5. How is the project creative?It turns a spreadsheet-style topic into a story. Resource management becomes an adventure with a map, an astronaut, and a minimap.It uses a "delayed consequence" mechanic. Choosing the quick fix feels good now but punishes the player later — a narrative device rarely used in educational games.It blends live and archived real data into gameplay, so the game feels connected to the actual universe, not a fictional one.It labels its own science. Separating recorded data, scientific models, and game simulation is a creative act of honesty that most games avoid.Historical Mode turns real NASA events into playable missions, each with a briefing that explains what actually happened.Communication delay is a gameplay mechanic. On Mars, asking Mission Control for help means the reply arrives two sols later — teaching signal lag through play, not text.6. What factors did the team consider?Age range and cognitive load. Younger players get fewer resources and simpler language; older players get the full system. This drove the two-difficulty design.Accessibility. Read-aloud support, large text in Cadet mode, keyboard navigation, and clear focus outlines.Scientific honesty. Every claim is labeled by source, and game numbers are explicitly marked as simplified.Reliability. Live APIs can fail, so archived fallbacks were built in from the start — the game must never crash in front of a player or a judge.Engagement vs. education balance. The game had to be fun first, or children won't play long enough to learn.Deployment simplicity. No accounts, no installs, no API keys — so it works in any browser immediately.Realism of consequences. Delayed penalties, resource drain, and communication delays were chosen because they reflect real space exploration challenges.
